strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: whether audio retrieval systems handle query reformulation, commands, and explicit exclusions. Separating target retrieval from distractor suppression is a useful evaluation perspective.

Experiments cover three datasets, four CLAP baselines, three backbone configurations, and adaptation with and without Clotho. The reported results support competitive T2A performance and specific advantages on imperative queries and HNSR@10, while acknowledging M2D-CLAP’s stronger average UIQ retrieval.

The paper provides useful implementation details, generation prompts, human validation, and inference measurements. Its investigation of training–evaluation overlap and stated use of exclusion blocklists are valuable methodological efforts.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior negation understanding is not isolated experimentally. HNSR@10 can improve through better matching of positive content or different distractor rankings without understanding the exclusion. The paper needs paired controls that remove or reverse exclusions, preferably with target–distractor roles swapped. Table 17 also shows that Robust-CLAP exceeds every OEA variant on mean rank separation, so superiority across discrimination metrics is overstated. No uncertainty estimates or per-dataset exclusion results establish the consistency of the reported gains.

The T2T experiment is insufficiently specified despite being a central contribution. Section 5.2 does not clearly identify the indexed captions, caption-generation model and prompt, query construction, relevance mapping, or prevention of identical captions appearing as both queries and candidates. These details are especially consequential for MECAT, described as having one auto-captioned pair per clip. Comparison only against CLAP text encoders also leaves the practical caption-indexed retrieval claim untested against dedicated text embedding models.

Benchmark validation does not establish either real-world representativeness or reliable exclusion labels. The 675 human ratings cover only 75 queries from 15 distinct clips, with only 15 negative queries. The interface emphasizes agreement with captions and makes listening optional; captions need not enumerate every audible event, so absence of an excluded sound requires stronger verification. Appendix I discusses real query lengths but supplies no measured UIQ length distribution. Moreover, Appendix D’s prompts omit the claimed vocabulary-grounding and ±2-word constraints, leaving the actual generation procedure unclear.

Reproducibility remains below the threshold for a clear Findings recommendation. Batch size, training epochs or step counts, learning-rate assignment by model/stage, scheduler, and early-stopping settings are absent. Hard-negative mining uses unspecified dynamic thresholds, and the extent and rejection rate of human verification are not reported. The release links are blank, the full benchmark is deferred until publication, and the MECAT reference lacks a usable identifier. Together with the missing T2T protocol, these gaps prevent independent reconstruction of the main results.

The causal and generalization claims exceed the comparisons. Vanilla versus adapted models establishes the value of retrieval training, but does not isolate shared-backbone architecture, instruction tuning, model size, or training data. Strong Clotho results after Clotho training do not demonstrate cross-domain generalization. Different dataset provenance and unspecified overlap checks also do not establish that MECAT is entirely contamination-free, particularly for pretrained backbones. The explanation that CLAP uses a bag-of-content representation whereas LLMs preserve structure through attention is technically misleading: CLAP text encoders also use contextual attention.

Several headline statements need qualification. The abstract’s 22% T2T gain is specific to MECAT against M2D-CLAP, rather than an overall gain against the strongest T2T baseline; Table 11 reports mean R@5 of 64.75 versus MGA-CLAP’s 62.32. The selected HNSR@10 and TFR@10 improvements also come from different OEA variants. The reported gains are promising, but clarifying the evaluation protocols and adding targeted exclusion controls are necessary before the central claims support publication.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: caption-style evaluation incompletely captures natural-language audio search, particularly commands and explicit exclusions. Evaluating successful retrieval jointly with distractor suppression is useful.

The experiments cover three datasets, four CLAP baselines, and multiple backbone configurations. The reported results support complementary strengths: OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) improves imperative-query R@5 from 44.74% to 49.87% and negative-query HNSR@10 from 30.3% to 34.6% over M2D-CLAP, while acknowledging that M2D-CLAP leads average UIQ retrieval.

The manuscript provides generation prompts, adaptation details, human validation, and inference measurements. Its investigation of WavCaps overlap with evaluation datasets and stated use of training blocklists are valuable methodological considerations.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior negation understanding is not isolated by the experiments. Better HNSR@10 can arise from improved matching of positive content or different ranking distributions without understanding exclusions. The paper needs matched queries with exclusions removed or reversed, and verification that excluded events actually distinguish the paired recordings. Caption dissimilarity and auditory confusability alone do not establish this. No uncertainty estimates accompany the reported gains.

The text-to-text evaluation, a principal contribution, is insufficiently specified. Section 5.2 does not explain which captions constitute queries and indexed documents, how identical-caption matches are excluded, or which automatic captioner and generation procedure are used. This is particularly consequential for MECAT, described as 847 audio-caption pairs. Strong text-embedding baselines are also missing, so beating CLAP text encoders does not establish the proposed architecture's advantage for caption-indexed retrieval.

Benchmark construction and validation leave substantial uncertainty. Only 15 underlying clips receive human validation, and audio inspection is optional; caption-based judgments cannot reliably establish the absence of excluded sounds. Appendix D's prompts omit the claimed vocabulary grounding and relative ±2-word constraint. Table 9 is described as queries for one clip but switches between barking, footsteps, and rain. Appendix I promises a token-distribution comparison but provides no measured UIQ distribution. These issues weaken both reproducibility and claims about realistic search behavior.

Important reproduction details are absent: batch sizes, training durations, per-model learning-rate choices, exact validation configurations, hard-negative filtering thresholds, and retained-pair counts. The resource links in the release statements are blank, while full benchmark release is deferred. The available methodological description therefore does not adequately support independent reproduction.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Clotho gains after Clotho training do not establish cross-domain generalization. Different source collections and unspecified overlap checks cannot guarantee that MECAT is contamination-free, especially with pretrained backbones. Comparisons across models with different pretraining and adaptation histories also do not isolate shared-backbone architecture or instruction-following as the cause of improvements.

The presentation overstates some results: the highlighted 22% T2T gain is specific to MECAT against M2D-CLAP, rather than an aggregate improvement or comparison with the strongest T2T baseline. The explanation that CLAP lacks compositional attention is unsupported. The supported empirical gains are promising, but clarifying the evaluation and adding targeted controls are necessary before a sound Findings recommendation; these revisions appear feasible for the next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: whether audio retrieval systems handle query reformulation, commands, and explicit exclusions. Separating target retrieval from distractor suppression is a useful evaluation perspective.

Experiments cover three datasets, multiple backbone configurations, and four CLAP baselines. The reported results show complementary strengths: OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) improves imperative-query R@5 from 44.74% to 49.87% and HNSR@10 from 30.3% to 34.6% relative to M2D-CLAP, while acknowledging M2D-CLAP’s stronger overall UIQ retrieval.

The paper includes useful implementation details, query-generation prompts, human validation, and inference measurements. Its explicit investigation of WavCaps overlap with evaluation datasets is particularly valuable.
weaknesses: The central claim of superior negation understanding is not isolated experimentally. HNSR@10 can improve through better matching of positive content or different ranking behavior without understanding the exclusion clause. Matched queries with exclusions removed or reversed, evaluated on the same target–distractor pairs, are needed. Caption dissimilarity also does not establish that the excluded sound is absent from the target and present in the distractor; the reported sampled human verification does not quantify this property.

The T2T protocol is insufficiently specified despite supporting a headline contribution. Section 5.2 does not establish exactly how indexed captions are obtained, which captioning model and settings are used, how multiple captions are handled, or how query–index overlap is prevented. This is especially consequential for MECAT, described as containing 847 auto-captioned pairs. Strong text-retrieval baselines are also missing, so outperforming CLAP text encoders does not establish that OEA is the preferred caption-indexed retrieval method.

Benchmark validity is narrower than the real-world robustness claims. Human validation covers only 15 clips and 75 distinct queries; 675 ratings are repeated judgments of these items. The criterion primarily assesses consistency with captions, rather than authentic search behavior or exclusion correctness. Appendix I discusses the published 1.8-token Freesound average but provides no actual UIQ length distribution. Moreover, Appendix D’s prompts do not encode the claimed vocabulary grounding and ±2-word constraint, leaving their enforcement unclear.

Important reproducibility information remains missing: effective batch size, stage-specific training schedules, learning-rate assignment, random seeds, exact baseline checkpoints, and numerical hard-negative filtering rules. The manuscript’s resource links are blank, and full benchmark release is deferred until publication. Appendix A provides useful architectural settings but does not resolve these gaps.

Several interpretations exceed the comparisons. Clotho gains from models explicitly trained on Clotho do not demonstrate cross-domain generalization, and MECAT T2A gains are small and inconsistent across variants. Different source datasets and unsuccessful overlap checks cannot establish that MECAT is entirely uncontaminated, particularly with respect to backbone pretraining. Likewise, the shared-backbone explanation is not isolated by an architectural ablation, and describing CLAP text encoders as lacking attention-based compositional processing is misleading.

No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or training-seed variability accompany the key gains. Claims of dominant T2T performance emphasize M2D-CLAP although MGA-CLAP is the stronger aggregate T2T baseline: the mean R@5 comparison is 64.75% versus 62.32%. The abstract’s +22% improvement is specific to MECAT against M2D-CLAP, rather than an overall improvement. These presentation issues require correction alongside the protocol and validation gaps. Collectively, the unresolved soundness and reproducibility concerns warrant revision next cycle rather than a positive Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: audio retrieval under varied linguistic formulations, including explicit exclusions. Separating target retrieval from distractor suppression provides a useful evaluation perspective.

Experiments cover three datasets, four CLAP baselines, three backbone configurations, and models with and without additional Clotho training. The reported results support competitive T2A performance and complementary gains on imperative queries and HNSR@10.

Appendix O provides valuable controls: removing exclusion clauses, shuffling identical tokens, and applying the same shuffle across models. The finding that exclusion clauses hurt every model, and that order sensitivity is shared with CLAP, usefully qualifies the original language-understanding hypothesis.

The manuscript reports inference costs, documents substantial benchmark overlap with WavCaps, and states that training blocklists were applied. These disclosures improve transparency about practical costs and evaluation risks.
weaknesses: The central T2T result is not reproducibly defined. Section 5.2 does not specify the gallery captions, caption-generation model and procedure, query/gallery separation, handling of multiple captions, or self-match exclusion. This is particularly consequential for MECAT, described as having one auto-captioned pair per clip. Comparisons only against CLAP text encoders also do not establish an advantage over dedicated text embedding models for the proposed caption-based pipeline.

Benchmark construction contradicts its stated controls. Section 3.2.2 claims vocabulary grounding and lengths within ±2 words of original captions, but Appendix D's documented prompts contain neither constraint and instead impose different fixed length ranges by query type. No enforcement procedure or achieved length statistics are supplied. Consequently, the claim that query formulation is isolated from vocabulary and length changes is unsupported.

Validation is too limited to establish the benchmark's broader real-world and exclusionary validity. The 675 ratings cover only 15 distinct audio clips and 75 queries; the evaluation primarily asks about agreement with captions, with listening optional and no explicit check that excluded sounds are absent from targets and present in distractors. Appendix L also incorrectly describes the reported human–LLM correlation of 0.89 as inter-annotator agreement. Controlled synthetic rewrites may be useful, but their representativeness of actual search behavior remains untested.

Important reproducibility details are missing: training batch sizes, stage durations, learning-rate assignments and schedules, exact validation splits, and final mining thresholds. Human threshold calibration lacks sample sizes and agreement results. Although code, checkpoints, and datasets are described as released, the supplied manuscript provides no usable resource URL; the release footnote ends without one.

Several numerical discrepancies require reconciliation. Table 15 gives OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) Δ-Rank as 29.8, whereas Table 18 reports 22.5 for the nominally corresponding exclusionary evaluation; HNSR@10 also changes from 34.6 to 34.4 without an explained protocol change. Table 19 reports 55.2 minus 60.5 as −4.6 rather than −5.3. These inconsistencies directly affect the mechanism analysis. Confidence intervals or paired tests are also needed for the headline retrieval and suppression improvements, beyond tests on embedding distances and shuffle effects.

The mechanism conclusion is stronger than the evidence. Larger target–distractor distances and corpus ranks show an association with audio-space separation, but do not establish that this chiefly causes the retrieval advantage; distances across independently learned spaces can reflect different geometry. Likewise, word shuffling establishes order sensitivity, not uniquely compositional exclusion understanding. The careful negative findings in Appendix O should more consistently constrain claims of superior semantic understanding elsewhere.

Generalization and contamination claims need qualification. Appendix B states that overlaps were blocklisted, while the main text and appendix still characterize AudioCaps and Clotho as contaminated without reporting residual overlap in the actual training subset. Different source datasets alone cannot establish that MECAT is entirely uncontaminated, especially with incompletely documented backbone pretraining. The strongest Clotho results additionally use Clotho training and therefore do not establish cross-domain generalization.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: evaluating audio retrieval beyond descriptive captions. Distinguishing target retrieval from suppression of a specified distractor is useful, and the proposed benchmark could support further research on query formulation and exclusion.

The empirical coverage is substantial: three datasets, multiple backbone sizes, four CLAP baselines, unadapted-model controls, and inference-cost measurements. The reported imperative-query and HNSR@10 improvements provide evidence of complementary strengths despite M2D-CLAP retaining the best average UIQ retrieval.

Appendix O provides valuable controls, particularly removing exclusion clauses and applying identical word shuffles across models. The authors explicitly acknowledge that exclusion clauses hurt all evaluated models and that sensitivity to word order is not unique to OEA.

The manuscript documents projection heads, LoRA settings, generation prompts, and evaluation metrics, and explicitly investigates training–evaluation overlap. These are useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline T2T contribution is insufficiently specified and contextualized. Section 5.2 does not identify the actual caption-generation configuration, explain gallery construction and handling of multiple captions, or establish separation between query text and indexed captions, especially for MECAT's auto-captioned pairs. These details are essential to interpret the large T2T gains. Moreover, comparisons against CLAP text encoders do not establish competitiveness with strong dedicated text retrievers. The highlighted 22% improvement is relative to M2D-CLAP on MECAT; MGA-CLAP is the stronger T2T baseline there and on average.

The exclusion results support better discrimination on the mined pairs, but do not establish superior exclusion understanding or the claimed causal mechanism. Removing the exclusion clause improves every model, including OEA. Word shuffling establishes order sensitivity but also produces unnatural text, so it does not unambiguously isolate semantic composition. Greater audio-space separation is correlational evidence, not proof that the audio branch chiefly causes the retrieval advantage; distances across separately trained spaces also reflect their different geometries. Controlled polarity reversals and queries requiring the exclusion clause to distinguish otherwise valid targets would strengthen the claim.

Benchmark validation is too limited for the stated real-world interpretation. The 675 human ratings cover only 75 distinct queries from 15 clips, including only 15 negative queries. Caption compatibility, with optional listening to the target, does not verify that excluded sounds are absent from the target and present in the distractor. Caption-length and vocabulary constraints also substantially restrict resemblance to natural search behavior. Appendix L incorrectly describes the reported human–LLM correlation of r = 0.89 as inter-annotator agreement, and its argument that selective model wins rule out generator bias is not convincing.

Important reproduction details remain missing or inconsistent. Training batch sizes, stage lengths, learning-rate assignments and schedules are unspecified; mining thresholds and the size/results of their human calibration are absent. The documented generation prompt does not include the claimed vocabulary-grounding and ±2-word constraints. The manuscript states that code, checkpoints, and datasets are publicly released, but provides no usable release link. These omissions materially affect reconstruction of both the model and benchmark.

The evaluation accounting needs reconciliation. Table 15 reports OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) Δ-Rank = 29.8, whereas Appendix O reports 22.5 without adequately explaining the change in evaluation population. Table 19 lists 55.2 − 60.5 as −4.6 rather than −5.3, affecting the subsequent structure-contribution calculation. The advertised HNSR, HNSR@10, and TFR@10 best values also come from different OEA variants and should be identified consistently. Main retrieval improvements lack confidence intervals or repeated-run estimates; significance tests on auxiliary embedding distances do not establish significance of these improvements.

Generalization and contamination claims need tighter qualification. Appendix B says overlap blocklists were applied, but does not clearly establish the resulting training counts and coverage for each evaluated checkpoint. MECAT's different source dataset alone cannot guarantee absence of shared web recordings or backbone pretraining exposure, and the reported embedding/filename checks lack sufficient detail. Clotho-trained variants cannot substantiate cross-domain generalization on Clotho, while MECAT gains are small and model-dependent. Taken together with the unresolved protocol and reproducibility issues, these concerns require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: caption-based audio retrieval benchmarks do not adequately test variation in search-query formulation. The UIQ taxonomy and paired target–distractor evaluation provide useful directions for multimodal retrieval research.

Experiments cover three datasets, four CLAP baselines, and six adapted model variants. Results support competitive audio retrieval and complementary strengths on imperative queries and hard-negative suppression, without claiming uniformly superior standard retrieval.

Appendix O provides valuable diagnostic controls. In particular, reporting that removing exclusion clauses improves suppression, and that word-order sensitivity also occurs in CLAP, usefully qualifies a simplistic explanation based on superior LLM negation understanding.
The manuscript documents training-data overlap, reports inference costs, and supplies architectural details and generation prompts. These disclosures improve the transparency of the study.
weaknesses: The central T2T result is insufficiently specified to assess or reproduce. Section 5.2 does not clearly identify the query/gallery construction, caption source or captioning checkpoint, handling of multiple captions, or exclusion of identical query–gallery text. Comparing only against CLAP text encoders also leaves the claimed practical advantage untested against strong dedicated text retrievers. These details and baselines are particularly important because T2T is a headline contribution.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the stated release: the manuscript provides no usable code, checkpoint, or dataset URL. Training descriptions omit batch size, stage lengths, learning-rate assignment, and seed information; the mining procedure omits its final thresholds and quantitative calibration results. The supplied generation prompt also lacks the vocabulary-reuse and caption-length constraints claimed in the main text.

UIQ validation supports caption consistency more directly than real-world search validity. Only 15 underlying clips, producing 75 queries, are evaluated, and listening is optional. This offers limited evidence that exclusion clauses accurately distinguish the actual audio pairs. Caption-length constraints and vocabulary reuse further limit representativeness of short natural searches. Appendix L additionally mislabels the human–LLM correlation reported earlier as inter-annotator agreement.

The mechanism evidence warrants narrower conclusions. Greater audio-only separation is consistent with improved discrimination but does not establish that it chiefly causes the retrieval gains; absolute cosine distances also depend on embedding geometry. Shuffling tests order sensitivity rather than isolating correct exclusion semantics. The finding that removing exclusions improves every model is important, but conflicts with stronger claims of superior semantic understanding elsewhere in the paper.

The leakage analysis is useful but leaves evaluation provenance unresolved. Appendix B says blocklists were applied, whereas the main discussion emphasizes contaminated benchmarks without clearly identifying the post-filter training counts and which reported runs used those filters. Distinct source datasets and unspecified similarity checks do not establish absence of overlap with all backbone pretraining data. Clotho improvements after Clotho training should also be distinguished from cross-domain generalization.

Several reporting inconsistencies require reconciliation. The headline HNSR@10, HNSR, and TFR@10 advantages select different OEA variants in Table 15; OEA-Qwen7B (+Cl) has TFR@10 of 9.8, not 10.1. Its negative-query rank gap also changes from 29.8 in Table 15 to 22.5 in Appendix O without a clear reconciliation. Main retrieval improvements lack uncertainty estimates. Together with the underspecified central evaluation, these are substantive issues preventing a sound Findings recommendation, but appear addressable in a revision for the next cycle.
